segments.title: Why the historical record becomes misty
segments.body: The view from a moving train supplies the metaphor. Nearby scenery is clear, just as relatively recent events can be studied through many sources and points of reference. Farther back, the record becomes obscured, accounts diverge, and missing pieces leave blank spaces. Historians try to fill those gaps by finding additional sources. Academic or professional training teaches that research skill, though sustained independent study and good resources can teach it too.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts plentiful recent sources with the missing and divergent evidence of more distant periods.

segments.summary: The "mists of time" describe an older historical record in which sources grow scarcer, accounts diverge, and gaps become harder to fill.

segments.title: Inference where the evidence has gaps
segments.body: Historical reconstruction resembles assembling a large jigsaw from a landscape partly hidden by fog. History follows systematic rules for gathering and analyzing evidence, yet it is still generally regarded as something other than a science because some reconstructions include jumps that cannot always be proved. A historian may have evidence on either side of a gap and infer what connects it without possessing the missing middle. The inference can be logical without becoming direct proof. That incompleteness creates both the mystery and the appeal of working through the "mists of time."

evidence.note: He compares historical reconstruction with a jigsaw and explains the limits of inference where the middle evidence is absent.

segments.summary: Historical interpretation resembles a jigsaw puzzle: evidence and disciplined analysis can support an inference even when the missing links cannot be proved.
